newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Former Pakistani spymaster protests Kansi arrest.
newsitem.headline: Former Pakistani spymaster protests Kansi arrest.

text.p: Pakistan's former military spymaster said on Sunday he would sue the government over the seizure and transfer to the United States of a Pakistani accused of deadly shooting outside CIA headquarters in Virginia.

General Hameed Gul, former director general of the military Inter Services Intelligence, told Reuters by telephone he would submit a petition to a high court on Monday about how Mir Aimal Kansi, 33, was captured and delivered to his accusers.
"I want to raise the sovereignty issue. The sovereignty of Pakistan has been violated," Gul said. "The law of land has been flouted with impunity as no legal requirements were fulfilled."
His voice was the latest to be heard in a storm of protest over the Kansi affair, which many politicians and ordinary people see as a national insult by Pakistan's powerful ally.
Gul, a fervent supporter of national and Islamic causes, argued that national sovereignty had been treasonably violated.
"If any elected representative, or whoever, or a head of government does something like this, it is unconstitutional and a constitutional writ is in order," he said.

Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's government, which has kept silent on the Kansi affair, is under fire from several religious and nationalist parties for its apparent collusion in the U.S.-led operation to spirit the wanted man out of the country.

Kansi is reported to have been grabbed from a hotel in the Punjab provincial town of Dera Ghazi Khan in the early hours of last Sunday by American agents of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, backed by Pakistani security men.
He was then flown from Islamabad to the United States in a U.S. military plane, apparently without a court hearing or any formal extradition procedures.
Badar-ul Islam, the commissioner, or top administrator, of Dera Ghazi Khan, told Reuters by telephone he believed Kansi had been the target of a high-level security swoop in his city.

"We were not in the picture at all. The entire thing happened in the dark, and we came to know in the morning that something happened last night. But something happened through use of force by an agency. We do not know which agency it was."

"Everybody is surmising it was Aimal Kansi," Islam said. "The surmise is correct I think, to a very large extent. It can't be anybody else. The streets were virtually streaming with vehicles, of a description not meeting our vehicles."

The FBI said on Tuesday that Kansi, a native of Pakistan's southwestern province of Balochistan, had been delivered abroad by unidentified Afghans to the custody of U.S. authorities and brought back to the United States to face trial.
FBI officials gave no details about Kansi's seizure and would not say if any of those involved would collect a reward of up to $2 million offered for the fugitive.
"The implications of the Kansi affair are profoundly disturbing for Pakistan and the Pakistani public," the English-language The News said in an editorial on Sunday.
"The Kansi case has brought to the fore troubling questions about national dignity, self-respect, the rule of law and, above all, national sovereignty," the daily added.
Gul, who was deeply involved in joint U.S.-Pakistani efforts to fund and arm Afghan guerrillas fighting Soviet troops in the 1980s, alleged that Kansi had illicit links with the CIA.
"I have raised the issue that he was a CIA contact, therefore he was guilty of breach (of the law) as far as Pakistan is concerned," he added.

Kansi is accused of being the gunman who shot five people, four of them CIA employees, outside the agency's headquarters in Langley, Virginia more than four years ago. Two of his victims were killed and three wounded.
